title: 巧加木头隔条  (Untangling the Lantern Cord)

segments.t: Up on the breezy second-floor balcony, Chen and Hao work shoulder to shoulder, drawing the two tangled lantern cords carefully back across the wooden railing. Listen first.
老陈，把左边那根绳轻轻往你那边拉——两个灯笼的铁丝提手钩住了。
慢慢来……把珊瑚色那个从金色上面绕过去，一下子就分开了。
一点儿纸都没破！不过明晚要是再刮风，这两条绳还是会碰在一起。
所以我才从地窖拿了四根轻便雪松木棍上来，两头都钻好了孔。
等等——你是说在两根平行绳子中间绑木头隔条，就像帆船缆绳那样？！
我叔叔年轻时修过码头的木船；两条平行线加上木隔档，怎么吹都不打绞。
让我把这根雪松木条绑在正中间——你看两条绳现在多稳当！
再给每个灯笼提手扣上个小铜环，这样哪盏都跳不出来。
老陈，这招建筑上和行船上都绝了——看它们一齐轻轻晃得多整齐！
对于一个连平板电脑都没有的老头来说，还算凑合吧，志豪？
老陈，每次跟你一块儿干活，我笔记本上都能多记一页！
走，下楼吧——前台还有三十个木衣夹等着小晴呢。
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
老陈，把左边那根绳轻轻往你那边拉——两个灯笼的铁丝提手钩住了。

'Pull the left cord gently toward you, Chen—two lanterns hooked their wire handles together.' "Tishou" names a carry handle ("ti" = lift + "shou" = hand), and "gouzhu" means snagged or hooked tight together.
慢慢来……把珊瑚色那个从金色上面绕过去，一下子就分开了。

'Easy does it... lift the coral globe up over the gold one, and they come apart cleanly.' "Manman lai" encourages patience ("take it slow"), while "yixiazi" highlights how swiftly ("in one clean motion") the handles separate.
一点儿纸都没破！不过明晚要是再刮风，这两条绳还是会碰在一起。

'Not a speck of torn paper! Still, if the wind blows tomorrow evening, these two lines will touch again.' "Yidianr ... dou mei po" underscores zero damage ("not even a tiny bit torn"), and "buguo" introduces a practical "however."
所以我才从地窖拿了四根轻便雪松木棍上来，两头都钻好了孔。

'That's why I brought up four light cedar dowels from the cellar with holes drilled at both ends.' Pairing "suoyi" with "cai" literally stresses "that is precisely why," while "zuanhao" means already neatly drilled.
等等——你是说在两根平行绳子中间绑木头隔条，就像帆船缆绳那样？！

'Wait—you mean tying wooden spacer bars between parallel cords like rigging on a sailboat?!' In "mutou getiao", "ge" ("separate") + "tiao" ("strip/bar") creates a clear compound for a wooden spacer bar.
我叔叔年轻时修过码头的木船；两条平行线加上木隔档，怎么吹都不打绞。

'My uncle worked on harbor wooden boats in his youth; two parallel lines with wooden spacers never twist.' "Zenme chui dou bu ..." means "no matter how hard it blows, they never..." and "dajiao" describes cords twisting around each other.
让我把这根雪松木条绑在正中间——你看两条绳现在多稳当！
'Let me tie this cedar bar right in the middle—look how steady both cords stay now!' Warm everyday word "wendang" means steady, reliable, and well-balanced—here praising how calmly both cords hang.
再给每个灯笼提手扣上个小铜环，这样哪盏都跳不出来。

'And snap a tiny brass ring onto each lantern handle so not a single one can jump loose.' "Koushang" means to clasp or latch shut, and "na zhan dou ..." ("whichever lantern, none...") ensures every single one stays put.
老陈，这招建筑上和行船上都绝了——看它们一齐轻轻晃得多整齐！

'Architecturally and nautically brilliant, Chen—watch them sway gently together in unison!' Informal praise "jue le" means "utterly brilliant," while "yiqi" means "all together in step" as the globes sway evenly ("zhengqi").
对于一个连平板电脑都没有的老头来说，还算凑合吧，志豪？
'Not bad for an old fellow who doesn't even own a tablet computer, eh, Hao?' Chen frames his point of view with "duiyu" ... "laishuo", and modest "couhe" downplays a clever fix as "passable enough."
老陈，每次跟你一块儿干活，我笔记本上都能多记一页！
'Every time I work alongside you, Chen, I get to add another page to my notebook!' Hao uses colloquial "yikuair" ("together") and pairs "duo" ("more") with "ji" ("jot down").
走，下楼吧——前台还有三十个木衣夹等着小晴呢。

'Come on downstairs—I have thirty wooden clothespins waiting for Qing at the front desk.' Tool compound "mu yijia" joins "mu" (wood) and "yijia" (clothes clip), while "dengzhe ... ne" pictures them sitting ready for Qing.

Wooden spacer bars keep the rooftop lanterns swaying smoothly together without a single tangle! See you next time.
再见！
